```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  prompt = FALSE
)
library(readjsa)

fixture <- function(name) {
  installed <- system.file("extdata", name, package = "readjsa")
  candidates <- c(
    installed,
    file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", name),
    file.path("inst", "extdata", name)
  )
  path <- candidates[nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates)]
  if (!length(path)) stop("The packaged fixture is missing: ", name)
  path[[1L]]
}

ivi_html <- fixture("ivi.html")
reos_html <- fixture("reos.html")
salm_html <- fixture("salm.html")
```

The current release catalogue is the contract between a publisher's page and
the parser. `jsa_release_manifest()` lists the supported dataset/family pairs
and the classification context that the parser will attach to observations.

```{r manifest}
jsa_release_manifest()
```

The manifest is deliberately more specific than a dataset name. IVI has six
layouts:

* `skill_states` — skill levels by state or territory;
* `anzsco4_states` — four-digit ANZSCO occupations by state or territory;
* `anzsco2_states` — two-digit ANZSCO occupations by state or territory;
* `anzsco2_ivi_regions` — two-digit ANZSCO occupations by JSA IVI region;
* `anzsco2_gccsa_sa4` — two-digit ANZSCO occupations by GCCSA/SA4; and
* `anzsco4_remoteness_northern` — four-digit ANZSCO occupations by JSA
  Remoteness and Northern Australia.

REOS is represented by the `reos_tables` family because its workbook's
`Information` sheet defines the table metadata. SALM has separate `salm_sa2`
and `salm_lga` families because their geography identifiers and ASGS vintages
are different. A family is not a cosmetic label: it selects the schema that
will be validated.

## Discover a catalogue without a network call

`discover_jsa_releases()` normally reads an official HTTPS publication page.
For tests and reproducible examples it accepts HTML text or a local HTML path.
The packaged pages below are deterministic shape fixtures, not live snapshots
of the publishers' production pages.

```{r offline-discovery}
ivi_catalogue <- discover_jsa_releases("ivi", html = ivi_html)
reos_catalogue <- discover_jsa_releases("reos", html = reos_html)
salm_catalogue <- discover_jsa_releases(
  "salm",
  html = salm_html,
  resource_html = list(
    salm_sa2 = fixture("salm_sa2_resource.html"),
    salm_lga = fixture("salm_lga_resource.html")
  )
)

catalogue_summary <- rbind(
  ivi = data.frame(dataset = "ivi", families = nrow(ivi_catalogue)),
  reos = data.frame(dataset = "reos", families = nrow(reos_catalogue)),
  salm = data.frame(dataset = "salm", families = nrow(salm_catalogue)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
catalogue_summary
```

The returned catalogue includes `source_url`, `source_filename`, reference
dates and, where the publisher page exposes them, release/vintage dates. It
also includes publication and terms URLs, licence text, and attribution.
The default `strict = TRUE` refuses a partial or ambiguous catalogue. That is
intentional: selecting "the first link" could silently mix families or
vintages. If a publisher changes its page, inspect the error and update the
catalogue handling rather than guessing a URL.

```{r catalogue-identities}
ivi_catalogue[c("family_id", "reference_period", "source_filename")]
reos_catalogue[c("family_id", "reference_period", "source_filename")]
salm_catalogue[c("family_id", "reference_period", "source_filename")]
```

## Parse the corresponding local shapes

The fixture workbooks and CSV demonstrate the parser entry points without
contacting a server. Real releases use the same family-specific entry points,
but their row counts and values change with each publication vintage.

```{r family-shapes}
ivi_skill <- read_ivi_file(
  fixture("ivi_skill_states.xlsx"), family = "skill_states"
)
reos_tables <- read_reos_file(
  fixture("reos_current.xlsx"), tables = c("1.1", "3.3")
)
salm_sa2 <- read_salm_file(fixture("salm_sa2.csv"), geography = "sa2")

data.frame(
  family = c("skill_states", "reos_tables", "salm_sa2"),
  rows = c(nrow(ivi_skill), nrow(reos_tables), nrow(salm_sa2)),
  columns = c(ncol(ivi_skill), ncol(reos_tables), ncol(salm_sa2)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

Use the fields retained by each parser rather than reconstructing source
meaning from column positions. For example, `classification_version` and
`geography_type` are the explicit geography/classification contract, while
`source_filename`, `raw_bytes`, and `raw_sha256` identify the exact file that
was parsed.

```{r family-columns}
list(
  ivi = c(
    "series_type", "occupation_level", "occupation_code",
    "occupation_title", "geography_type", "geography_code"
  ),
  reos = c(
    "table", "series", "frequency", "unit", "table_title",
    "table_definition", "disaggregation_group", "disaggregation"
  ),
  salm = c(
    "geography_type", "geography_code", "geography_name", "data_item",
    "classification_version", "observation_status"
  )
)
```

When you need a current release, use `read_ivi()`, `read_reos()`, or
`read_salm()` with the family/table/geography selection. When you need an
offline or pinned replay, save the catalogue row, fetch the raw file once, and
call the corresponding `*_file()` parser with the saved provenance. The next
article demonstrates that pattern without using a live endpoint.
